questions.stem: What is the standard, internationally accepted SI (International System of Units) unit for measuring heat energy in physics?

options.option_text: Calorie
Joule
Watt
Kelvin

questions.explanation: Heat is a form of energy. Therefore, like all other forms of energy (and work), its SI unit is the Joule (J). A calorie is an older, non-SI unit of heat. Watt is the unit of power, and Kelvin is the SI unit of temperature.

questions.stem: The standard normal core body temperature of a healthy human being is approximately 37°C. What is this exact equivalent value on the Fahrenheit scale?
questions.explanation: Using the conversion formula: °F = (°C × 9/5) + 32. So, (37 × 9/5) + 32 = 66.6 + 32 = 98.6 °F. This is why a body temperature above 99°F or 100°F is usually considered a fever.

The Second Law of Thermodynamics (Kelvin-Planck statement)

questions.explanation: Ignoring the padded distractors: The Second Law of Thermodynamics establishes the concept of entropy and inefficiency. It dictates that some heat must always be rejected to a cold sink; therefore, a perfectly efficient (100%) heat engine is impossible in the real universe.
